title: BUS 1600 — The Whole Semester, Out Loud

lines.t: Okay. Seven weeks, thirteen sessions, two credits, and fifty-five percent of your grade sitting in exactly two places. This is the marketing episode.
And the good news is that the course is smaller than it looks. Four frameworks carry almost all of it. If you know those cold, everything else is detail.
So that is what we are going to do. The grade, the four frameworks, then the sessions, then the case, and we finish with a self-test you can answer out loud.
Nothing here replaces the reading, and you write the case yourself. But by the end of this you should be able to walk into a lecture already knowing where it fits.
Start with the grade. Where does it actually come from?
Two things decide it. The midterm case write-up is thirty percent. The final exam is twenty-five. Together that is fifty-five percent of your grade in two deliverables.
And the other forty-five?

Four group assignments at five percent each, so twenty. Attendance is ten. An individual assignment is ten. Research participation, the SONA sessions, is five. Plus a two percent extra credit plan on Starbucks if you want it.
Here is the part I want people to hear twice. Attendance and SONA together are fifteen percent, and neither one requires you to study anything.
Call it the free fifteen. Show up, do the sessions, and you have banked it. Skip them and an A quietly becomes a B without you ever failing anything.
Tell me about the SONA trap, because this one is genuinely unforgiving.

There are two windows. September eighth to the seventeenth, and September twenty-ninth to October eighth. You must attend once in each window. Doing two sessions inside one window only earns you half — two and a half percent.
And if you miss the first window entirely?
The full five percent is gone permanently. There is no making it up later. Put both windows in your calendar today.
Late work?

One to seven days late costs you twenty percent. Eight to fourteen days costs fifty. Past fourteen days is a zero. And nothing at all is accepted after October thirteenth at eleven fifty-nine at night.
One more, on the honour code, because it is specific.

Do not upload the course text or the Harvard cases to a language model. And if you do use A I anywhere, cite it to the original source, not to the model. Study from a guide all you like. Write the case yourself, from the case P D F.
Right. Framework one. The five Cs.

This is the situation map. Before you decide anything, you describe five things. Customers, collaborators, competitors, company, context. The company sits in the middle and the other four are the world around it.
Give me the question each one asks.

Customers — whose needs are we fulfilling, how big are they, how do they buy. Collaborators — who helps us create value, so suppliers, retailers, agencies. Competitors — who else is chasing the same need in the same customers. Company — our own resources, skills, offering, goals. Context — the economy, technology, regulation, culture.
And there is one of those that students consistently get wrong.
Competitors. Almost everyone writes down other firms in the same industry. That is not the definition. A competitor is anyone fulfilling the same need for the same customer.
The example that makes it stick?

Netflix. Netflix's competitor was never only Blockbuster. It was sleep. It was video games. It was going out on a Friday night. If you had written down only the video rental chains you would have missed the entire market.
Let us run the five Cs on the case you actually have to write. Opera Philadelphia.

Customers — aging subscribers, plus a young audience that attends occasionally. Collaborators — the Academy of Music, the donors, the festival venues. Competitors — every other Friday night in Philadelphia. Company — mid-sized, a bold artistic reputation, thin margins. Context — post-pandemic arts attendance, streaming, and an aging donor base.
Notice he did not say other opera companies for competitors.
Because they are not the threat. The threat is a couple deciding to stay home.
Framework two. The three V principle.

This is the viability test. An offer only survives if it creates value for all three parties at the same time. Customer value above zero, and collaborator value above zero, and company value above zero.
Walk the legs.

Customer value is benefits minus price — is this worth more to me than what I give up. If that is negative, nobody buys. Collaborator value is enough margin and enough reason for partners to carry it, ship it, stock it, promote it. If that is negative, nobody sells it. Company value is profit, share, or strategic position. If that is negative, we cannot sustain it.
And two out of three?

Two out of three is a bankruptcy. The case is MoviePass. Ten dollars a month for unlimited films — enormous customer value. Theatres got paid full price, so real collaborator value. Company value was deeply, structurally negative. It was never going to work, and the three V test tells you that on day one.
This is the fastest test to run on any business idea.
Including your own. If a friend pitches you something, ask which of the three legs is negative. There is almost always one.
Framework three. The seven marketing tactics.

This is Chernev's update of the old four P's. Seven dials, grouped by what they do. Five design the offering — product, service, brand, price, incentives. One communicates it — communication. One delivers it — distribution.
Say that grouping again, because that is how it gets tested.
Design — product, service, brand, price, incentives. Communicate — communication. Deliver — distribution.
And there is a comparison from lecture two that shows one tactic deciding an entire industry.
Netflix against Blockbuster. Blockbuster did not lose on price. It did not lose on advertising. It lost on two tactics — distribution and brand.
Distribution first.
Slow to embrace streaming. Difficult to collaborate with. Chronic new-release shortages. Netflix was flexible on all three.
And brand.
Blockbuster was a bricks-and-mortar retailer defined, in the customer's mind, by late fees. Netflix was entertainment, and it embraced the disruption.
Now here is the detail I love. Late fees are filed under brand, not under incentives.

And that is the whole lesson. A pricing-and-incentives decision became the single association customers held about the company. One badly set tactic reached across and redefined a different box entirely. So when you analyse a firm, walk all seven. Every time.
Framework four. SWOT. Which feels like the easy one and apparently is not.
It is easy until you have to place things. Strengths and weaknesses are internal — about the company. Opportunities and threats are external — about the world.
And Professor Hogue flagged the exact mistake he sees.
Putting external forces into strengths, or company facts into opportunities. On the ECOALF assignment, strengths and weaknesses are internal to ECOALF only.
So try one. Consumers increasingly prefer sustainable fashion. Where does that go?
Opportunity. It is external — it is a fact about the world, not about ECOALF.
But that is only half marks.

Right. He wants the derivative opportunity. Not that the trend exists, but what that trend specifically lets ECOALF do next — a virtual store, a persistent-trend product line. Go one step past the observation and you are writing at the level he grades at.
Session two. Value. And apparently he opens by complaining about the word.
His line is that value is a highly over-used term in marketing. So he defines six versions of it, and you should expect a short answer question asking you to distinguish two.
Give me the pair most likely to be asked.

Value chain versus value delivery network. The value chain is Porter — all the activities inside your own company that add value, design through to delivery. Apple: chip design, assembly, retail store, the Genius Bar. The value delivery network is wider — you plus your suppliers, distributors and customers, improving the whole system together. Toyota and its tier-one supplier network.
Inside the firm, versus the whole ecosystem.
That is the sentence. And a third one, value migration, is economic value shifting away from stale business models toward more agile ones — value moving from cable bundles to streaming.
Now the number I actually need to be able to compute. Customer lifetime value.
Simple version. Average revenue per year, times gross margin percentage, times the average number of years you keep them.
Work it.

A streaming subscriber at fifteen dollars a month. That is a hundred and eighty dollars of revenue a year. At a sixty percent gross margin, a hundred and eight dollars of profit a year. Keep them three and a half years on average, and lifetime value is three hundred and seventy-eight dollars.
And what does that number license you to do?

It is the ceiling on acquisition spend. You can spend up to three hundred and seventy-eight dollars to acquire one and break even. If your actual cost to acquire is a hundred and twenty, each subscriber nets you about two hundred and fifty-eight.
Every is this campaign worth it question reduces to that.
Every one.
Customer centricity. Definition, please.
Seeing the world in general, and a company's services in particular, from the customer's point of view.
And the four A's.
Sheth and Sisodia. Acceptability, affordability, accessibility, awareness. They are the four management failures behind most business failures — an offer that fails any one of them fails.
Give me a product for each failure. Or at least one good one.
Google Glass. Awareness was enormous — everyone had heard of it. Accessibility was fine, you could buy one. It failed acceptability. People did not want to be seen wearing it.
Last thing in this session, and it is the one that makes a good short answer.

The counterpoint. Marshall Field said the customer is always right. Bezos says start with what the customer needs and work backwards. But Herb Kelleher at Southwest said the customer is sometimes wrong, and defending an abusive customer over your own employee is a betrayal of that employee.
So customer centricity starts where?
With employees. That tension is the answer to the question, not a problem with it.
Session three. Marketing research. And I want to start with what it is for, because I think people get this wrong.

Research rarely finds you the next big thing. That is the honest version. What it does, done well, is focus the debate on strategy — it shortens timelines and raises confidence. Done badly it is a disaster, and speed to market is no excuse for negligence.
Three types. How do I pick?

Qualitative when the issue is not well understood, or the answer needs no number — testing a product name, for instance. Quantitative when you need a measurable answer you can project to a population. Observational when you need a compelling reason to believe, drawn from what people actually did.
Say the split in one line, because that is the exam answer.
Qualitative tells you why, and cannot be projected. Quantitative tells you how many, and can. Observation tells you what people actually did, rather than what they said.
Primary and secondary data.

Primary is freshly gathered for your project — expensive, slow, exactly on-question. Kantar, Ipsos, Morning Consult. Secondary already exists, collected for someone else's purpose — cheap, fast, not on-question. Nielsen, I R I, Mintel.
Sampling plan. Three decisions.
Sampling unit — whom do we survey. Sample size — how many. Sampling procedure — how do we choose them.
And the sample size question that shows up as arithmetic.

Error falls with the square root of n. So going from a hundred respondents to five hundred more than halves your error. Going from one thousand to two thousand buys you less than a single point, for double the money.
So if I have five hundred and I want to halve my error?
You need about two thousand. Four times the sample. That trade-off is the entire reason research budgets get argued about.
Conjoint. Why is it better than just asking people what they would pay?

Because asking what you would pay produces a fantasy. Conjoint forces trade-offs between whole competing offers, the way a real purchase works. You pick four to six attributes with levels — price points, ad-free or limited, digital or digital plus print.
And people do not have to see every combination.
A fractional factorial or orthogonal design shows each respondent a statistically valid subset — five to fifteen choice tasks — so they do not fatigue but the statistics still hold.
What comes out of it?

Part-worth utilities — a number for how much each attribute level contributes to preference. And then preference share simulation, which predicts the market split for a product that does not exist yet.
One more, on A B testing, because there are five steps and he will want all five.
Formulate the hypothesis. Isolate one variable. Define your success metrics up front. Execute a fifty-fifty split launch to similar audiences. Analyse and iterate.
And why does it work?
Because only one thing changed, the difference in results is the effect of that thing. Change two variables and you have learned nothing at all.
Session four. S T P. And you told me this is the highest-leverage session in the course.

It is. The midterm rubric names segmentation and brand positioning explicitly, the Opera Philadelphia case is about segmentation, and the syllabus tells you to review the segmentation workbook carefully. If you only deeply learn one session, learn this one.
The three steps.

Segment — cut the market into groups that would genuinely respond differently. Target — pick which of those to serve, based on size, growth, fit with your strengths, and competitive intensity. Position — decide the single idea you want to own in that segment's head, relative to competitors.
Four ways to cut a market.
Demographic, geographic, psychographic, behavioural. And behavioural — usage rate, occasion, loyalty, benefit sought — is usually the most predictive of the four.
What makes a segment worth targeting?

Four tests. Measurable, so you can size it. Substantial, so it is worth chasing. Accessible, so you can actually reach it with media and distribution. Actionable, so you can build something different for it.
And the line I want people to write down.
A segment you cannot reach is a fact, not a strategy.
The positioning statement template.
For target segment, who need or occasion, brand is the frame of reference that point of difference, because reason to believe.
And perceptual maps. What does empty space mean?
Either an opportunity, or a place nobody wants to be. Your job in the write-up is to say which, and why. Never just point at the gap.
Case tip, before we move on.

When you name your target segments for Opera Philadelphia, name them by behaviour and motivation. Lapsed single-ticket buyers who came for a festival production. Not twenty-five to forty-four year olds. Then show the marketing mix changing for that specific group. That is what insights beyond the obvious means in the forty percent rubric line.
Sessions five and six. Consumer behaviour, then behavioural economics.
The core idea of session five is that buying is a process, not a moment. Five stages, and each one has its own lever — so identifying the stage tells you which tactic to pull.
Walk the five with the levers attached.

Problem recognition — the lever is communication that names the need. Information search — S E O, reviews, retail presence. Evaluation of alternatives — positioning, brand, price. Purchase — incentives, distribution, checkout friction. Post-purchase — service, loyalty, lifetime value.
And the four influences on the buyer.

Cultural — the slowest-moving and strongest. Social — family, reference groups, status, which is why influencer marketing works. Personal — age, life stage, occupation, lifestyle. Psychological — motivation, perception, learning, memory, beliefs.
Now behavioural economics. Ariely's argument in one line.

Standard economics assumes people are rational utility maximisers. They are not. They are predictably irrational. And the consequence for a marketer is that how you frame an offer changes demand as much as the offer itself.
Three biases. One line each.

Anchoring — the first number seen sets the reference point. A twelve hundred dollar list price makes seven hundred feel like a deal, regardless of what the thing is worth. Loss aversion — losing a hundred dollars hurts about twice as much as gaining a hundred pleases, which is why do not lose your streak beats earn a reward. And the decoy effect — adding an obviously worse third option changes which of the other two people pick.
Give me the Economist numbers, because this is the best example in the course.

Three options. Web only at fifty-nine dollars. Print only at a hundred and twenty-five. Print plus web, also a hundred and twenty-five. With all three on the page, sixteen percent chose web only and eighty-four percent chose print plus web. Nobody at all chose print only.
So remove the one nobody chose.
And the winner flips. Web only jumps to sixty-eight percent, print plus web collapses to thirty-two, and revenue falls.
Which means what?
An option nobody buys can still be the most profitable thing on the menu — because its only job is to make another option look obviously correct.
And one warning on the likely exam question here.

It will probably be: give an example of a behavioural bias and how a marketer would use it ethically. Note the word ethically. Ethical influence is a stated goal of the course, so the boundary is part of the answer, not decoration.
Session seven. Digital. And this is where the arithmetic lives.
Digital gets its own session because it is the only channel where every stage of the funnel is measured. Which makes it the place marketing has to prove return on investment.
Four formulas. Say them.

Click-through rate is clicks divided by impressions. Conversion rate is conversions divided by clicks. Cost per acquisition is spend divided by conversions. And return on marketing investment is incremental revenue, times contribution margin, minus spend — all divided by spend.
Work the whole funnel, slowly.
A hundred thousand impressions produce two thousand clicks. Two thousand over a hundred thousand is a two point zero percent click-through rate.
Next.
Those two thousand clicks produce sixty signups. Sixty over two thousand is a three point zero percent conversion rate.
Spend was three thousand dollars.
Three thousand divided by sixty conversions is a fifty dollar cost per acquisition.
And the return.

Sixty signups at a hundred and eighty dollars of first-year revenue each is ten thousand eight hundred dollars. At a sixty percent contribution margin that is six thousand four hundred and eighty. Subtract the three thousand of spend, and divide by the three thousand of spend. That is one hundred and sixteen percent return on marketing investment.
And the caveat you must add.

That is year one only. Lifetime value runs three and a half years. So the campaign is considerably better than a hundred and sixteen percent over the life of those customers — and saying that sentence is what separates a good answer from a correct one.
Three quick concepts to close the session.

Owned, earned and paid media. Owned is your site and your list, and it compounds. Earned is press, reviews, word of mouth. Paid is advertising, and it stops the day you stop paying. Attribution — last-click is easy and wrong, because it over-credits search and under-credits awareness. And close-loop analysis — evaluate results, improve the creative, run the next campaign, and log everything so targeting improves each cycle.
Sessions eight through twelve. The back half walks the mix, one dial at a time. Let us go quickly.

Product first. A product is three things at once. The core benefit — the need it solves. The actual product — features, quality, design. And the augmented product — warranty, service, delivery, community.
And the strategic point?
Competitors copy the actual product. They rarely copy the augmented one. That is where defensible advantage tends to live.
Product life cycle.

Introduction, growth, maturity, decline. The stage dictates the tactic. Heavy advertising to build awareness in introduction. Distribution and line extensions in growth. Defend share and cut cost in maturity. Harvest or discontinue in decline. Naming the wrong tactic for the stage is the classic wrong answer.
Branding. Define brand equity.
The extra value the name adds beyond the physical product. It is why someone pays more, searches for you by name, or forgives you a mistake.
Keller's pyramid, bottom to top.

Salience — who are you, do they know you exist. Performance and imagery — what are you, function and meaning. Judgments and feelings — what do I think and feel about you. And resonance — loyalty, community, advocacy. You cannot skip a level.
What destroys equity?
Constant discounting, which teaches people to wait. Inconsistent messaging. Line extensions that blur what you stand for. And service that contradicts the advertising.
Pricing. The title of the session is pricing beyond cost, which is basically the argument.

Cost tells you the floor. Competitors tell you the ceiling. Only the customer tells you the right price. Cost-plus ignores what people would happily pay and leaves money on the table. Competition-based ignores your own differentiation and invites a price war. Value-based pricing starts from perceived value and works backwards — and that is the one he teaches.
Elasticity, quickly.

Percentage change in quantity divided by percentage change in price. If the absolute value is greater than one, demand is elastic and a price cut raises total revenue. If it is less than one, demand is inelastic and a price rise raises total revenue.
Work the example.
Raise price ten percent, volume falls four percent. Minus four over ten is minus zero point four. Absolute value below one, so inelastic, so revenue rises.
And distribution, which is the tactic that killed Blockbuster.

Distribution is availability. A product the target cannot conveniently get does not exist to them — that is the accessibility A from the four A's. Channel levels: zero-level is direct, full margin and full data and full control, but you fund the whole thing. One level adds a retailer — more reach, shared margin. Two levels add a wholesaler as well — widest reach, thinnest margin, least control of the shelf.
Push and pull.

Push means you market to the channel — trade deals, slotting fees, sales incentives — so retailers stock it and push it. Pull means you market to the end customer so they walk in asking for it and the retailer has to stock it.
And intensity.

Intensive is everywhere — Coke. Selective is chosen outlets — Levi's. Exclusive is one per territory — luxury cars. And intensity has to match positioning, because luxury sold everywhere stops being luxury. That sentence connects distribution back to brand equity, which makes it an excellent short answer.
Now the thing that is worth thirty percent. The case.

Opera Philadelphia, due September fifteenth at eleven fifty-nine. Maximum three pages of text plus exhibits, minimum ten point font. The graded deliverable is the write-up, not your in-class presentation.
Five sections. What does each one have to do?

Section one, executive summary. Three moves inside it — the hook, which is the most pressing challenge or opportunity. The ask, which is what decision is needed now. And the bottom line, which is your recommendation with the facts behind it. Write this section last.
Section two.
Situational diagnosis — the why. And the instruction here is blunt: do not summarise the case. The executives know their own history. Analyse the market using the five Cs and SWOT.
Section three.
Strategic alternatives. The case gives you three. Evaluate them, and say plainly which one you recommend. Do not hedge.
Section four.

Recommendation and implementation — the how. Three to four recommendations. Name the target segments, drawing on the segmentation workbook. Apply the seven tactics where they are relevant — you do not have to use all seven.
And section five, which you said people skip.

Risk mitigation. The top two risks of your recommendation, and how the company pivots if either happens. He is an economist by training, and the whole course is framed around digesting and managing risk. A C-level deliverable without a risk section is incomplete.
How is it scored?
Analytical rigor forty percent. Strategic alignment thirty. Correct use of concepts twenty. Professionalism ten.
Define the big two.

Rigor means deep use of the five Cs, the marketing mix, segmentation, targeting, brand positioning and SWOT — with insight beyond the obvious. Alignment means the analysis actually supports the recommendation, and the recommendation can actually be implemented.
His three stated tips.

One — think like an owner. What is your guidance to the Executive Director and his team. Two — the so what test. Every exhibit and every data point must lead to a decision or an insight. If it does not, cut it. Three — persuasion, not description. Not the market is growing, but we must capture the fifteen percent growth in the millennial segment before a competitor builds brand loyalty there.
Hard constraints, so nobody loses points on a technicality.

Stay inside the case timeframe — no hindsight, no data the case does not contain. No outside research, and no consulting former students. Do not upload the case to a language model. And three pages of text maximum, with exhibits supplemental and not counted.
Give me a structure that reliably scores.

Page one, executive summary and diagnosis. Page two, alternatives plus your three to four recommendations mapped to specific tactics. Page three, implementation timing and risks. Exhibits — the segment table, a SWOT box, and a positioning map. And give every exhibit a one-line caption stating the decision it supports. That is the so what test made visible on the page.
Alright. Self-test. Twelve questions. I will ask, you get a few seconds, then you hear the answer. Say it out loud — it works better.
One. Name the five Cs, and say which one students most often define too narrowly.
Customers, collaborators, competitors, company, context. Competitors is the one. It means anyone fulfilling the same need for the same customer, not just firms in your industry.
Two. An offer delights customers and pays partners well, but loses the company money. What does the three V principle say?
It is not viable. All three legs must be positive at the same time. Two out of three is MoviePass.
Three. List the seven marketing tactics in their three groups.
Design — product, service, brand, price, incentives. Communicate — communication. Deliver — distribution.
Four. Which two tactics explain Blockbuster's failure?
Distribution and brand. Slow to streaming, hard to collaborate with, new-release shortages — and a bricks-and-mortar retailer defined by late fees.
Five. On a SWOT for ECOALF, where does consumers increasingly prefer sustainable fashion go, and why do students get it wrong?
Opportunity — it is external. Strengths and weaknesses are internal to ECOALF only. And the graded answer pushes further to the derivative opportunity, like a virtual store.
Six. Difference between value chain and value delivery network.
Value chain is Porter — activities inside your company, design to delivery. Value delivery network is the broader ecosystem of you, suppliers, distributors and customers improving the whole system.
Seven. A customer generates a hundred and eighty dollars a year at sixty percent margin and stays three and a half years. What is lifetime value, and what does it tell you?

A hundred and eighty times zero point six is a hundred and eight a year. Times three and a half is three hundred and seventy-eight dollars. It is the ceiling on what you can sustainably spend to acquire that customer.
Eight. Name the four A's, and give a product that failed one.
Acceptability, affordability, accessibility, awareness. Google Glass had awareness and accessibility but failed acceptability — people did not want to be seen wearing it.
Nine. Give the five steps of an A B test.
Formulate the hypothesis, isolate one variable, define success metrics, execute a fifty-fifty split launch, analyse and iterate. Primary metrics are click-through rate and conversion rate.
Ten. Why is conjoint better than asking what would you pay?
It forces real trade-offs between whole competing offers, mirroring an actual purchase. And it predicts preference share for products that do not exist yet.
Eleven. You have five hundred respondents and want to halve your margin of error. What does that cost?
About two thousand respondents — four times the sample — because error falls with the square root of n. That diminishing return is the core sampling trade-off.
Twelve. Nobody chose the print-only option at a hundred and twenty-five dollars. Why keep it on the page?
Because its presence made print plus web at the same price look obviously superior, moving choice from thirty-two percent up to eighty-four. An option nobody buys can still drive the most revenue.
That is the course. Four frameworks, twelve sessions, one case.
If you are short on time before the final, do two passes. One through the four frameworks, and one through the case playbook. Those two carry most of the points.
And check Brightspace weekly. The syllabus itself says Brightspace is always the most current source for what is due.
Good luck with the case. Write the risk section.
